existing_incident_edges.relationship: Critical fabulation confronts the violence of slavery’s archive while requiring narrative restraint and acknowledging the failure to recover the dead (2008).
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Hartman’s pp.9 and 11–14, read. She distinguishes speculation from verified recovery and refuses closure; no claim that invention supplies lost testimony is accepted. This personal methodological contribution is different from the existing aggregate archive-to-Atlantic and archive-to-Black-history arrows.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Wayward Lives (2019) places ordinary young Black women’s experiments in living at the center of historical explanation, while refusing to reproduce state case files’ pathologizing judgments.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: The book’s method is read through Hartman’s 2020 first-person interviews and the 2019 institutional account, not a new whole-book reading. This contribution concerns women’s history and its subjects; the generic archive/Atlantic relationships are retained separately.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Hartman admires Du Bois’s intellectual achievement but criticizes the Philadelphia survey’s elite and Victorian judgments about Black intimate life (2020 interview).
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Explicit first-person answer to Yannise Jean about Du Bois, read. The criticism is dated to the 2020 interview and limited to these class/gender judgments, rather than a wholesale rejection of Du Bois or a passage independently checked in the 2019 book.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Hartman’s “Venus in Two Acts” is explicitly named as inspiration for Connolly and Fuentes’s 2016 slavery/archive special issue, as Fuentes reports in 2017.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Fuentes’s AAIHS essay explicitly identifies Hartman’s essay as inspiration. Fuentes’s author bibliography establishes Connolly’s coeditorship and 2016; USF corroborates their joint introduction in Fall 2016. Influence is limited to that collaborative project, not Hartman as sole source of Fuentes’s work or agreement on every method. The full issue remains unread.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Hartman cites Silencing the Past while questioning whether obeying historical conventions consigns captive girls to oblivion.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own Venus 2008, 9–10/n32 cites Trouillot alongside Stephan Palmié. The manufactured-certainties phrase belongs to Palmié 94; Trouillot is a see-also resource, not source of every sentence or sole origin of critical fabulation. Complete article 11–14 insists on restraint, irrecoverability and failure; not restoration of otherwise unknowable voices. Her cited 1997 manifestation is retained.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Roach’s account of Nash’s interpretation places Hine’s culture of dissemblance alongside Hartman’s critical fabulation in a genealogy of Black feminist thinking about archival violence and speculative historical practice.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Roach 2020:517 explicitly reports Nash rooting contemporary archive questions, including Hartman’s 2008 critical fabulation, in Hine’s earlier concept. This is an attributed analytic-predecessor comparison with double mediation (Roach→Nash), not direct Hartman testimony, demonstrated personal transmission, mentorship or identity of the two concepts. Roach references 519 identifies Venus in Two Acts; Nash only opening 519 read, 520–523 unread; Hartman original not read in this packet. Parent’s separate Trouillot→Hartman primary route remains distinct.

named_group_routes.relationship: The archive of Atlantic slavery as the field's hardest case: Hartman's 'Venus in Two Acts' (2008) and the 'critical fabulation' the MacArthur Foundation describes (2019); Fuentes's Dispossessed Lives (2016), which 'interrogates the archive and its historical production' for Bridgetown's enslaved and free women (publisher)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: MacArthur's description of critical fabulation (read); Fuentes's publisher description (read). Hartman and Fuentes unread. Trouillot's clauses were removed after review (finding 9): p4A_rel_21 carries them.

named_group_routes.relationship: Hartman's 'critical fabulation' and Fuentes's black-feminist reading of 'fragmentary sources' (2016) take the archive's violence as the problem of Black history
named_group_routes.evidence_note: MacArthur's description (read); Fuentes's publisher description (read). The black entry's strand archives ('Collecting and diaspora bibliography') is the hook. Trouillot's clause was removed after review (finding 9): p4A_rel_25 carries it.
